```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaFin)
```

`cudaFin` is a downstream example of the `rcupp` framework for finance-style
workloads. It refits a lasso on successive rolling windows of a feature
matrix and returns one-step-ahead forecasts. Like `cudaBio`, it has no CUDA
code of its own and works with either `rcupp` backend.

## A rolling forecast

```{r rolling}
set.seed(1)
n <- 80L
p <- 5L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
y <- drop(X %*% c(2, -1, 0, 0, 0)) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)

f <- rolling_predict(X, y, window = 30L, lambda = 0.01)
head(f$pred, 5)
```

The returned list holds the forecasts (`pred`), the realized values
(`actual`), the coefficient path (`coefficients`), plus summary statistics:

```{r summary}
f$mse
f$dir_acc
dim(f$coefficients)
f$backend
```

`mse` is the mean squared forecast error and `dir_acc` is the fraction of
steps where the predicted direction matched the realized one. The
`coefficients` matrix has one column per forecast step, so it shows how the
fitted signal evolves over the rolling windows.

## Choosing the window and the penalty

`window` sets the number of past observations used for each fit, `lambda`
controls the penalty, and `n_iter` the number of solver steps per window.
Smaller windows adapt faster but are noisier, while a larger `lambda` drives
more coefficients to zero. Because each fit is cheap, both can be tuned by a
direct sweep. We use a larger simulated sample with a known sparse signal:

```{r tuning-data}
set.seed(11)
n <- 120L
p <- 6L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
beta_true <- c(1.2, -0.8, 0, 0, 0.5, 0)
y <- drop(X %*% beta_true) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)
```

```{r window-sweep, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
windows <- c(20L, 30L, 40L, 60L, 80L)
mse_w <- vapply(windows, function(w) {
  rolling_predict(X, y, window = w, lambda = 0.02, n_iter = 100L)$mse
}, numeric(1))
round(mse_w, 3)

plot(windows, mse_w, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "Window length", ylab = "Forecast MSE",
     main = "Effect of window length")
```

Longer training windows give lower error because the lasso estimate is less
noisy; the gain tapers off once the window is long enough. The penalty sweep
shows the usual bias-variance trade-off:

```{r lambda-sweep, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
lambdas <- c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.6)
mse_l <- vapply(lambdas, function(l) {
  rolling_predict(X, y, window = 40L, lambda = l, n_iter = 100L)$mse
}, numeric(1))
nonzero <- vapply(lambdas, function(l) {
  fit_l <- rolling_predict(X, y, window = 40L, lambda = l,
                           n_iter = 100L)
  mean(colSums(fit_l$coefficients != 0))
}, numeric(1))
sweep <- rbind(mse = mse_l, nonzero = nonzero)
colnames(sweep) <- lambdas
round(sweep, 3)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1) + 0.1)
plot(lambdas, mse_l, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "lambda", ylab = "Forecast MSE", main = "Accuracy")
plot(lambdas, nonzero, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "darkorange",
     xlab = "lambda", ylab = "Mean non-zero coefficients",
     main = "Sparsity")
par(op)
```

Moderate values of `lambda` prune irrelevant features at little cost in
accuracy, while a very large penalty removes real signal and inflates the
error. See `?rolling_predict` for the full argument list.

## Visualizing the forecasts

A single fit is easiest to read as a time series:

```{r main-fit}
f <- rolling_predict(X, y, window = 40L, lambda = 0.02, n_iter = 100L)
c(mse = f$mse, dir_acc = f$dir_acc)
```

```{r forecast-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(f$actual, type = "l", col = "grey40", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Forecast step", ylab = "Value",
     main = "Predicted vs actual")
lines(f$pred, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("actual", "predicted"),
       col = c("grey40", "darkorange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The `coefficients` matrix has one column per forecast step, so plotting it as
an image shows how each feature's weight evolves as the window rolls forward.
The three signal features keep large, stable weights; the others stay near
zero.

```{r coef-path, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
nr <- nrow(f$coefficients)
nc <- ncol(f$coefficients)
image(seq_len(nc), seq_len(nr), t(f$coefficients), axes = FALSE,
      xlab = "Forecast step", ylab = "Feature",
      col = hcl.colors(32, "Blue-Red 3"), main = "Coefficient path")
axis(1)
axis(2, at = seq_len(nr), labels = seq_len(nr), las = 1)
box()
```

## Reproducibility and the pure-R reference

`rolling_predict()` is fully deterministic: the step size uses the fixed
Lipschitz bound `1 / sum(Xw^2)` and `n_iter` is fixed, so the same inputs give
bit-identical results on every backend.

```{r reproducible}
f2 <- rolling_predict(X, y, window = 40L, lambda = 0.02, n_iter = 100L)
identical(f$pred, f2$pred)
identical(f$coefficients, f2$coefficients)
```

That determinism makes the compiled path easy to audit against a short pure-R
implementation of the same ISTA contract. Repeating the first window's fit by
hand reproduces its coefficients to machine precision:

```{r pure-r-ref}
ista_ref <- function(Xw, yw, lambda, n_iter) {
  step <- 1 / sum(Xw^2)
  thresh <- lambda * nrow(Xw) * step
  beta <- rep(0, ncol(Xw))
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    r <- (yw - as.vector(Xw %*% beta)) * step
    u <- beta + as.vector(crossprod(Xw, r))
    beta <- sign(u) * pmax(abs(u) - thresh, 0)
  }
  beta
}
w <- 40L
Xw <- X[seq_len(w), , drop = FALSE]
beta_ref <- ista_ref(Xw, y[seq_len(w)], 0.02, 100L)
max(abs(f$coefficients[, 1] - beta_ref))
```

The package test suite extends this comparison to the whole forecast path.
That is why the results plotted above can be trusted on both the CUDA backend
and the CPU fallback.
